Multiple shooting

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-multiple-shooting.Rmd
methods-multiple-shooting.Rmd

Single shooting integrates from the initial state over the whole time axis. For oscillating or spiking systems the objective is rugged: a parameter change shifts every later period, and a peak moved by more than the peak width leaves the residuals without direction, so few starts reach the narrow valleys. trust() offers multiple shooting instead (trust region).

Usage

Multiple shooting is a control of the objective:

obj <- normL2(data, g * x * p, multipleShootingControl = TRUE)
fit <- trust(obj, start)
fit$multipleShooting$violation
controls(obj, "multipleShootingControl") <- NULL   # single shooting again

The chain must be g * x * p with one Xs() built on odemodel(..., includeTimeZero = FALSE). Not available with it: hessianMethod = "exact", qnControl$hessianInit = "exact", several phases, switches, hessianReseed, qnMemory, nonmonotone, boundary = "clip", minimize = FALSE, traceFile.

entry of multipleShootingControl default controls
nodes "auto" "auto", "transitions", or node times
growth, misfit 10, 3 thresholds at which "auto" cuts a segment
minPoints states + 1 data points per half of a cut
charts all linear "log10", "linear" or "angle" per state
scale from the data scale of the gaps and node steps
init "data" node values: "data", "spline", "simulation" or a list
breaks none node times without continuity
entry of stepControl default controls
acceptance "filter" "filter", "merit" or "natural"
soc TRUE second-order correction of a rejected step
anneal TRUE penalty on the gaps raised in stages
twoPhase, restore, regularize off further globalizations

converged = TRUE requires the scaled gaps below tolControl$ctol. The result has a list multipleShooting with nodes, gaps, violation and the counts of the globalization.

Segments and gaps

Multiple shooting [1], [2] cuts the time axis at nodes \(\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_M\) and integrates segment \(j\) from node values \(s_j\), the first from the initial state of the parameter transformation. Continuity becomes the constraint

\[c_j = x(\tau_{j+1};\, \tau_j, s_j, \theta) - s_{j+1} = 0 . \tag{1}\]

Observed states start at the data, so every segment stays close to the data it covers for any parameters. At convergence the trajectory is continuous and the result is a stationary point of the single-shooting objective.

Condensed step

Bock’s generalized Gauss-Newton method linearizes (1). With the end-state sensitivities \(G_j = \partial x_j / \partial s_j\) and \(P_j = \partial x_j / \partial \theta\),

\[\Delta s_{j+1} = \alpha\, c_j + G_j\, \Delta s_j + P_j\, \Delta \theta , \tag{2}\]

and the recursion gives \(\Delta s = \alpha z + S\, \Delta\theta\). Substituted into the linearized residuals it leaves a Gauss-Newton model in \(\Delta\theta\) alone (condensing), of single-shooting size, so subproblem solver and bounds of trust() apply unchanged. The nodes follow the step by the linearization, not by simulation, so the gaps close only at convergence.

The trust region bounds parameters and nodes together,

\[\lVert D^{-1} \Delta\theta \rVert^2 + \lVert V (\alpha z + S\, \Delta\theta) \rVert^2 \le r^2 , \tag{3}\]

with \(D = \operatorname{diag}(\lvert v \rvert^{1/2})\) for the distances \(v\) to the bounds of Bound constraints, the identity without bounds, since a region on \(\theta\) alone leaves \(S\, \Delta\theta\) unbounded, which is huge across a spike. \(V\) is one over the state scale (multipleShootingControl$scale): data range for observed states, simulation range otherwise, a decade for log10 node values. \(\alpha = 1\) closes the linearized gaps (Bock’s step); under an active region \(\alpha \le 1\) is the share of the node part of the full step that the radius allows. A link of the condensing chain that would propagate a gap through expanding segments beyond a bound is dropped for the step. Other summands, a prior or a single-shooting normL2(), enter with value, gradient and Gauss-Newton Hessian.

control effect
stepControl$acceptance = "filter" (default) filter of Fletcher and Leyffer [3] on the objective function \(\mathcal{J}(\theta)\), \(-2 \log L\) or \(-2 \log\) of the posterior, and the scaled gap size \(h = \lVert V c \rVert\)
stepControl$acceptance = "merit" \(\ell_2\) exact penalty \(\mathcal{J} + \mu h\)
stepControl$soc (on) one second-order correction of a rejected step whose gaps did not close as predicted
tolControl$ctol converged = TRUE only for \(h\) below it; stagnation, rmin, ten failed solves in a row, iterlim, and under acceptance = "natural" a zero full step or one failed solve end the run with converged = FALSE above it
hessianMethod = "gn" condensed Gauss-Newton blocks
hessianMethod = "bfgs", "sr1" one quasi-Newton block per segment Lagrangian, from gradients alone, so usable with sweep = "reverse"

With open gaps the nodes absorb what the parameters do not explain, so the data term does not measure the fit.

Continuity annealing

From a distant start the condensed step can be forced through a regime the data never show, such as a spike threshold. stepControl$anneal (on) therefore first minimizes

\[\mathcal{J} + w \lVert V c \rVert^2 \tag{4}\]

over parameters and nodes on the sparse Gauss-Newton matrix, \(w\) rising tenfold per stage from one, then hands over to the exact method: precision annealing [4] with a fixed schedule. A stage ends when a step gains less than a thousandth of the objective; annealing ends early where a whole stage no longer closes the gaps. It needs forward sensitivities.

Node placement

multipleShootingControl$nodes = "auto" (default) starts from ten segments per condition, or one per half oscillation of the data if more, and halves a segment where

  • the spectral radius of \(G_j\) exceeds growth (default 10), the expansion of the linearized flow in the coordinates of the nodes;
  • the RMS of the weighted residuals exceeds misfit (default 3) and twice the condition median;
  • or the solve fails.

Cuts happen before the first step and at every iterate, never below half the finest data spacing, and keep minPoints (default: states plus one) data points per half, so no node fits a segment alone.

Over a period an oscillator has growth near one; what grows is the phase sensitivity to the frequency, linearly in the periods, until the segment fits the data a period off. One segment per half oscillation, counted at turning points of the data, bounds that slip. A misfit on every segment, from wrong parameters, cuts nothing, since no node removes it.

setting node values
charts = c(phi = "angle") gap counted modulo \(2\pi\)
charts entry "log10" node values of a positive state on the log scale
default observed states at the data; others from a run with observed states reset to the data at each data time, replacement synchronization [5]
init = "spline" smoothing spline, roughness by generalized cross-validation [6]
init = "simulation" simulation at the start parameters
list as fit$multipleShooting$nodes given values, node times in nodes

Under replacement synchronization, driven states such as a voltage-gated variable forget their start and follow the measured trajectory.

nodes = "transitions" puts a fixed node just before every fast change (a spike, the jump of a relaxation oscillator), a run of samples whose rate lies more than eight times mad(), the median absolute deviation scaled to a normal standard deviation, off the median rate, keeps the even nodes of ten segments where no change is near, and does not cut segments during the fit. Without a fast change in the data it is "auto". Each change then starts in the segment where the data have it, and a wrong timing shows as a gap before the next node. Numeric node times, for all conditions or as a list by condition, fix the layout.

Further step controls

stepControl$acceptance = "natural" selects Bock’s natural level function [7]: the full Gauss-Newton step damped by a factor from a curvature estimate, cut back by a corrector, and accepted when the simplified step at the trial point (current Jacobians, trial residuals and gaps) has shrunk. The filter takes over where the damping finds no step. It needs the Gauss-Newton Hessian, a fixed sigma and no error model.

Off by default, since each helps on some problems and costs on others:

control effect
stepControl$twoPhase fit parameters with nodes held at the start [6], then lay out nodes at the result and release them; helps with noisy node values, as on spiking traces, at several times the cost elsewhere
stepControl$regularize fix condensed directions with singular value below that fraction of the largest [7]
multipleShootingControl$breaks nodes without continuity constraint [8]; Gauss-Newton Hessian only
stepControl$restore filter restoration, at most five times: close the linearized gaps, damped if needed, else put the nodes on the current trajectory; on noisy spike trains this makes the layout cut more segments and fewer starts succeed

FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillator

The FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillator [9],

\[\dot V = c\,(V - V^3/3 + R), \qquad \dot R = -(V - a + b R)/c , \tag{5}\]

is fitted to the voltage \(V\) alone, 81 points on \([0, 20]\) with noise of 0.1.

fhnDir <- file.path(tempdir(), "fitzhughNagumo")
dir.create(fhnDir, showWarnings = FALSE)
fhn <- eqnvec(V = "c*(V - V^3/3 + R)", R = "-(V - a + b*R)/c")
fhnModel <- odemodel(fhn, modelname = "fhn_ode", includeTimeZero = FALSE, compile = FALSE,
                     outdir = fhnDir)
fx <- Xs(fhnModel, options = list(atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10))
fg <- Y(c(y = "V"), f = fx, modelname = "fhn_obs", compile = FALSE, outdir = fhnDir)
fp <- P(eqnvec(V = "V", R = "R", a = "a", b = "b", c = "exp(lc)"), condition = "C",
        modelname = "fhn_p", compile = FALSE, outdir = fhnDir)
compile(fx, fg, fp, output = "fhn", cores = 6)
fhnPrd <- fg * fx * fp

fhnTruth <- c(V = -1, R = 1, a = 0.2, b = 0.2, lc = log(3))
tt <- seq(0, 20, by = 0.25)
set.seed(1)
yy <- fhnPrd(tt, fhnTruth, deriv = FALSE)[[1]][, "y"]
fhnData <- as.datalist(data.frame(name = "y", time = tt, value = yy + rnorm(length(tt), 0, 0.1),
                                  sigma = 0.1, condition = "C"))
fhnSS <- normL2(fhnData, fhnPrd)
fhnMS <- normL2(fhnData, fhnPrd, multipleShootingControl = TRUE)

Forty starts perturb the initial states by a standard deviation of 1.5 and \(a\), \(b\), \(\log c\) by 1.

set.seed(7)
fhnStarts <- parframe(do.call(rbind, lapply(1:40, function(i)
  fhnTruth + c(rnorm(2, 0, 1.5), rnorm(3, 0, 1)))))
fhnFit <- function(obj, ...)
  as.parframe(mstrust(obj, center = fhnStarts, cores = 4, iterlim = 300, ...))
fhnRuns <- list("single shooting" = fhnFit(fhnSS),
                "multiple shooting, filter" = fhnFit(fhnMS),
                "multiple shooting, merit" = fhnFit(fhnMS, stepControl = list(acceptance = "merit")))

A hit has a single-shooting objective within 0.1 of the best, evaluated anew because open gaps can report a data term below the optimum.

fhnRuns <- readRDS("results/fitzhughNagumo.rds")
fhnValue <- function(f) apply(as.matrix(f[, names(fhnTruth)]), 1, function(th)
  fhnSS(th, deriv = FALSE)$value)
fhnBest <- min(unlist(lapply(fhnRuns, fhnValue)))
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fhnRuns), function(method) {
  f <- fhnRuns[[method]]
  hits <- sum(fhnValue(f) <= fhnBest + 0.1)
  data.frame(method, converged = sum(f$converged), hits, medianEval = stats::median(f$neval),
             evalPerHit = if (hits > 0) round(sum(f$neval) / hits) else NA_real_)
}))
#>                      method converged hits medianEval evalPerHit
#> 1           single shooting        19   17        301        424
#> 2 multiple shooting, filter        37   37         38         74
#> 3  multiple shooting, merit        36   36         38         88

Multiple shooting reaches the optimum from more than twice as many starts, at a sixth of the evaluations per hit. Most missed single-shooting starts hit the iteration limit; the three missed multiple-shooting starts take almost a third of the multiple-shooting evaluations, annealing included. An evaluation covers the time axis once, as in single shooting, plus the node-value sensitivities. Filter and merit function reach the optimum from nearly as many starts at a similar cost.
